clue.text: Hamlet’s first speech interrupted another character (7)

indicators.note: the first letter of Hamlet
the speech is cut off before its last letter

blocks.note: ORATION with its last letter cut off

explanation.surface: The prince opens his mouth on stage and another player cuts across him.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the surface: Horatio is another character in Hamlet, Hamlet's loyal friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Horatio is a character in Hamlet besides the prince himself.

clue.text: Naturally growing old interfered with racing (7)

indicators.note: letters that are interfered with are tampered with and rearranged

explanation.surface: An ageing racehorse, or its owner, gets meddled with at the track.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Growing' looks like it belongs with 'old', as in growing old; it is really part of the definition, Naturally growing.
explanation.definitionFit: Organic produce is grown naturally, without artificial chemicals.

clue.text: Warning from distant relative rebuffed (5)

indicators.note: the answer is taken from inside the words that follow
pushed back, so the letters run backwards (up, in a down clue)

blocks.note: the letters sitting across distanT RELAtive

explanation.surface: A family member you rarely see sends a warning and gets snubbed for it.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the two words and runs backwards, which is why it is hard to spot on the page.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an alert is a warning signal, as in a flood alert.

clue.text: Painting I think about no more (7)

indicators.note: IMO goes about, around, the next piece

blocks.note: IMO = in my opinion, text-speak for I think

explanation.surface: Someone says they have given up thinking about art.
explanation.walkthrough: IMO is modern texting shorthand that setters now use freely. Impasto is paint laid on thick enough to stand out from the canvas.
explanation.definitionFit: Impasto is a style of painting with thickly applied paint.

clue.text: Opening B&B after Union admitted one wouldn’t be welcome locally (3,4)

indicators.note: after means following in order, so the Bs are written behind the U
to admit is to let in, so the opening takes the other letters inside

blocks.note: a pore is a small opening in skin
the two Bs taken as they stand

explanation.surface: A bed and breakfast opens, and someone is turned away by the neighbours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening' looks like a verb about launching the guest house; it is a noun, PORE. 'Locally' means at the local, a British word for a neighbourhood pub.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub bore talks too long at the local, so nobody there is glad to see him.

clue.text: Release one French rugby player (6)

blocks.note: a lock is a second-row forward in rugby

explanation.surface: A French club lets one of its rugby players go.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a transfer: releasing a French rugby player. Lock is a rugby position, one of the two tall forwards in the second row of the scrum.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: unlocking a door or a prisoner's chains sets something free.

clue.text: Shooter turned up after strapping fellow wearing underwear (3,6)

indicators.note: after means following in order, so CAME is written behind OX
what is worn goes round the wearer, so BRA wraps the pair

blocks.note: an ox is a big, strong man

explanation.surface: A burly man in his underwear turns up, and someone is shooting at him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' looks like a reversal instruction; it just means CAME. 'Strapping' also teases the bra's straps.
explanation.definitionFit: A box camera is a simple camera, and cameras shoot pictures.

clue.text: A little narrow-minded in judging crosswords (7)

indicators.note: only a little of the word is taken, its first letter
N goes inside the next piece

explanation.surface: Someone is being a bit petty about how crosswords are judged.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is split: read 'crosswords' as cross words, angry words, which is what ranting is.
explanation.definitionFit: Ranting is angry speech, cross words.

clue.text: Clanger! Typist accidentally reveals where lovers are meeting (8,5)

indicators.note: the letters have been jumbled by accident

explanation.surface: A typist's slip in some letter lets out the secret of where two lovers meet.
explanation.walkthrough: A clanger is British slang for an embarrassing blunder, which is just what a typo is.
explanation.definitionFit: A tryst is a secret lovers' meeting, so the trysting place is its venue.

clue.text: Search for information out of turn – not a good look? (4)

indicators.note: GO is taken out of the search word

explanation.surface: Someone checks a fact at the wrong moment and it goes down badly.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is playful: an ogle is a look, and not a nice one, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The question mark flags a playful definition: an ogle is a leering stare, the opposite of a good look.

clue.text: First Mrs Vlad occupying a place in government – bewildering! (10)

indicators.note: EX occupies the space inside the other letters

blocks.note: the setter's first wife would be his ex
per = a, as in ten pounds per head
PL = place, as in street names

explanation.surface: The setter's former wife has landed a government post, to general bafflement.
explanation.walkthrough: Vlad is the setter, so Mrs Vlad is his wife and his first one is now his ex. 'A place in government' looks like one phrase but is four small pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean confusing enough to leave someone at a loss.

clue.text: Cross-country guest forced to leave golf links (6)

indicators.note: cross means angry, so the letters are in a temper and scrambled
G is made to go from the word

blocks.note: GUEST without G, golf in the radio alphabet

explanation.surface: An angry rural visitor is ordered off the golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Golf links' reads as one phrase, a golf course, but the split falls between them: golf is G and links is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To link things is to unite them.

clue.text: Used actors’ piece occasionally as a way of teaching (8)

definitions.note: Socratic is an adjective; the definition describes a teaching method rather than naming it

indicators.note: used means worn and knocked about, so the letters are disordered
only now and then a letter is taken, every other one

blocks.note: second and fourth letters of pIeCe

explanation.surface: A drama teacher uses bits of actors' scripts now and then in class.
explanation.walkthrough: The Socratic method teaches by asking questions, after the Greek philosopher Socrates.
explanation.definitionFit: Socratic describes teaching by questioning, Socrates' method.

clue.text: Grain perhaps and where to store it round highly secure location (9)

indicators.note: the store is turned round

blocks.note: grain is a crop, one example of one
grain is stored in a silo

explanation.surface: A farmer describes the harvest and the building that holds it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Highly' is literal: an acropolis is a citadel on high ground, as in Athens.
explanation.definitionFit: An acropolis is a fortified citadel on a hill, secure and high up.

clue.text: Birds over the road getting bread (9)

blocks.note: bread is slang for money, so riches

explanation.surface: Birds fly across the street to peck at bread someone has thrown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread' looks like bird food but is the old slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the ostrich is one kind of bird, the largest alive.

clue.text: Reported denial that comes straight from the horse’s mouth (5)

definitions.text: that comes straight from the horse’s mouth

indicators.note: a report is spoken, so the word is heard, not seen

explanation.surface: A denial that a journalist says is straight from the horse's mouth, the best source.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Straight from the horse's mouth' is an idiom for reliable news; here it is literal, the sound a horse makes.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful literal reading of the idiom: the sound a horse makes really does come straight out of its mouth.

clue.text: What unsubtle actors do with direction – test the limit of patience (5)

indicators.note: the limit, the end, of patience is its last letter

blocks.note: the MOT is the UK's annual roadworthiness test for cars

explanation.surface: A director's note: overacting tests everyone's patience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Direction' suggests a stage director; here it is only a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: To emote is to show feeling theatrically, as hammy actors do.

clue.text: Old dramatist in Hackney perhaps depressed (7)

indicators.note: in means inside, so LOW is placed within the horse

blocks.note: a hackney is a breed of horse, so perhaps a mare

explanation.surface: An Elizabethan playwright sits gloomy in the East London borough of Hackney.
explanation.walkthrough: Hackney looks like the London borough; it is also a breed of horse, and 'perhaps' flags it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Christopher Marlowe was an Elizabethan playwright.

clue.text: Roaming round country as its leader, some might say (9)

indicators.note: the letters are turned round and rearranged

explanation.surface: A leader travels round the country he runs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Its leader' is the leader of the country just clued, the US, and 'some might say' admits the dig is an opinion.
explanation.definitionFit: Critics of the American president might call him an ignoramus.

clue.text: One not in favour of bringing up Vennells’ former business model (7)

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing letters up reverses them

blocks.note: Paula Vennells ran the Post Office, the UK postal network, until 2019
a model poses, so a poser

explanation.surface: Someone objects to raising the old business model of Paula Vennells, of the Post Office scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Business model' reads as one phrase but splits: the business is the Post Office, and the model is a poser.
explanation.definitionFit: An opposer is someone against a proposal.

clue.text: Where to stand conveniently keeping in range (7)

indicators.note: the range keeps IN inside it

blocks.note: the Urals are a mountain range

explanation.surface: Advice on where to stand to keep within firing range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conveniently' is the pun: a convenience is a British word for a public toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Urinals are where men stand in a public convenience.

clue.text: Writer gets a lot of credit for being imaginative (6)

indicators.note: most of the word, all but its last letter

blocks.note: Edgar Allan Poe, the American writer
TICK, British slang for credit (on tick), losing its last letter

explanation.surface: An author wins praise for their imagination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Credit' looks like praise; it is TICK, as in buying on tick, meaning on credit.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: writing that is poetic is full of imagination and imagery.

clue.text: Blubber once when affected in Rialto (5,3)

indicators.note: the letters are affected, altered

explanation.surface: Someone once wept in Venice, moved on the Rialto bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blubber' looks like the verb, to weep; it is whale fat, and train oil is the old name for oil boiled from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Train oil was oil rendered from whale blubber, an old term.

clue.text: Expert parking? One’s over edge of driveway (6)

indicators.note: the unit lies over the D, covering it
the edge of driveway is its first letter

blocks.note: P = parking, as on road signs

explanation.surface: An expert on parking, whose car overhangs the driveway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Expert parking?' looks like a boast about parking; the question mark ends the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a pundit is a learned authority, these days often a TV commentator.

clue.text: Human failing in book (5)

indicators.note: the word falls apart and is reassembled

explanation.surface: A human flaw described in a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Human failing' reads as one phrase, a weakness; 'failing' is the anagram instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Nahum is one of the minor prophets' books in the Old Testament.

clue.text: Backing band stays for game of bridge (10)

indicators.note: the band is backed, turned back to front

explanation.surface: A backing band stays on to play at a bridge evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' looks like the card game; Poohsticks, from Winnie-the-Pooh, is played by dropping sticks off a bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: The game from Winnie-the-Pooh: players drop sticks off one side of a bridge and watch which floats out first.

clue.text: Get better describing Meghan’s number 2 – Prince Harry (4)

indicators.note: to describe is to draw round, so HAL goes round the E
the second letter of Meghan

blocks.note: Prince Hal, Shakespeare's name for the young Henry V

explanation.surface: A wish for Meghan's husband, Prince Harry, to recover.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface picks today's Prince Harry; the wordplay wants Shakespeare's Prince Hal, the future Henry V. Meghan's number 2 looks like her husband, but it is her second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a wound heals as it gets better.

clue.text: On the drink but not feeling great (7)

definitions.text: On the drink but not feeling great

blocks.note: reads as boozing, but the drink is slang for the sea, so this is being at sea
reads as a hangover, but is the nausea of a rough crossing

explanation.surface: Someone drinking heavily and feeling rough for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the drink' suggests boozing; the drink is also slang for the sea, and being ill at sea is being seasick.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone seasick is at sea and feeling ill.

clue.text: In short Starmer’s point accepted – we assume it’s true (7)

blocks.note: Starmer is Prime Minister, the premier, cut short

explanation.surface: A news line: the Prime Minister's argument has been conceded.
explanation.walkthrough: Keir Starmer is the UK Prime Minister, the premier.
explanation.definitionFit: A premise is a statement assumed to be true as the basis of an argument.
